variants.name: JDK dynamic proxy (java.lang.reflect.Proxy)
variants.implementation_notes: Proxy.newProxyInstance generates, at runtime, a class that implements the listed interfaces and dispatches every call to a single InvocationHandler.invoke, so one handler proxies any interface - the mechanism behind Spring AOP, mock frameworks and RPC stubs. It requires an interface (class proxying needs bytecode tools such as ByteBuddy or CGLIB), and the handler must also deal with equals/hashCode/toString. The classic static forwarding class remains the right variant when the proxy must expose a concrete type, when reflection overhead or JIT profile pollution matters, or when per-method compile-time-checked forwarding is wanted.
pitfalls: hashCode/equals/toString are dispatched to the handler as well; forgetting them yields surprising behavior (equals comparing handlers, toString leaking the handler class).
Checked exceptions from the target arrive wrapped in InvocationTargetException, undeclared ones in UndeclaredThrowableException - unwrap before rethrowing.
Proxy classes are generated per classloader and can pin classloaders and metaspace; cache proxy instances rather than creating them per call.
A dynamic proxy is not an instance of the concrete subject class, so instanceof/casts to the class fail.

variants.name: Static forwarding proxy class
variants.idiom_name: hand-written class implementing the Subject interface
variants.implementation_notes: The GoF form in Java source: a final class implements the Subject interface, holds the real subject and forwards each method, with the policy written inline. It costs one method per subject operation and must be kept in step with the interface, but it exposes a real type, is fully checked by the compiler, is immune to reflection overhead, and works on every Java version. Choose it when the proxy is part of the public API or when only a few operations need interception.
pitfalls: Default and new interface methods must be implemented or forwarded explicitly; an interface change breaks the proxy at compile time (which is the point, but it is real work).
The proxy is a different class from the subject, so equality, hashing and synchronization must be delegated deliberately if callers compare or lock on the subject.
